title: De insigni paradoxo, quod in analysi maximorum et minimorum occurrit

deep.reconstruction:
Context (E735, §§9–12): Euler studies the functional ∫√x ds, which he calls the 'momentum' of a curve. Here x is the depth below a fixed horizontal line ff…hh. Its extremals are parabolas whose directrix is that line. Physically, ∫√x ds is the Maupertuis–Euler action of a projectile whose speed is that acquired by falling from the line. In Euler's coordinates the parabola is x = a + y²/(4a), so the half-distance from the line to the vertex is a. The vertex-to-point value of the functional is (2/3)(2a+x)√(x−a).

The endpoints F and H lie at depths f and h, with horizontal separation 2g. On the previous page Euler finds a = gg/(f+h+2r), where r = √(fh−gg). He also finds √(af−aa) = −g(f+r)/(f+h+2r) and √(ah−aa) = g(h+r)/(f+h+2r). The minus sign means the vertex lies between F and H.

This page:
1. Subtracting the two vertex-based values gives the arc FH. Using 2a(f+h+2r) = 2gg, M(FH) = (2g/(3√a))·N/D, with N = 2gg+ff+hh+(f+h)r and D = f+h+2r.
2. Rationalize by multiplying top and bottom by f+h−2r, using r² = fh−gg.
3. The new denominator is (f+h)² − 4(fh−gg) = (h−f)² + 4gg.
4. The new numerator is (f+h)(2gg+ff+hh) − 2(f+h)(fh−gg) + (2fh−ff−hh−4gg)r. This equals (4gg+(h−f)²)(f+h−r).
5. The common factor cancels, so M = (2g/(3√a))(f+h−r).
6. With √a = g/√(f+h+2r): M(FH) = (2/3)(f+h−r)√(f+h+2r).

§13: because r carries a ± sign, two extremal parabolas join F and H when gg < fh. These are the two projectile trajectories from F with launch speed √(2·g_grav·Ff) that hit H, i.e. the high and low throws. No real extremal exists if gg > fh, since H is then out of range.

The next page (§14–15) treats gg = fh. The two solutions merge on the envelope (the 'safety parabola'), giving M = (2/3)(f+h)^{3/2}. This exceeds the broken path F→f→h→H, whose value is (2/3)(f^{3/2}+h^{3/2}). That broken path is a discontinuous, Goldschmidt-type minimum running along the zero-cost line x = 0.
errors: Previous-page formula contains the misprint f√(af−hh) for f√(af−aa); this does not propagate.
On this page the algebra checks: the numerator and denominator after rationalization, and the final value (2/3)(f+h−r)√(f+h+2r), are all correct.
Euler does not say which sign of r gives the smaller value. With s = f+h, dM/dr = −3r/√(s+2r) < 0, so the +r branch has the smaller momentum and the −r branch the larger one.
Euler does not identify that the other arc is not a minimum at all (it passes the envelope/conjugate point).

ideas.what: Closed-form value of the action ∫√x ds along the two parabolic extremals between two given points: (2/3)(f+h∓r)√(f+h±2r), with r = √(fh−g²)
ideas.modern_name: Value function / action of projectile trajectories (Jacobi metric √(E−V) ds)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Routine computation; the action principle itself is due to Maupertuis/Euler (1744)
ideas.where_published: E735 (Opera postuma); the ∫√x ds = projectile-path link appears in Euler's 1744 Methodus inveniendi, Additamentum II

ideas.what: Two extremals through two points when gg<fh, none when gg>fh, merging at gg=fh (the envelope/maximum-range trajectory)
ideas.modern_name: Envelope of extremals, conjugate points, Jacobi condition; safety parabola
ideas.usually_credited_to: Jacobi 1837 (conjugate points); envelope theorem by Darboux/Kneser/Zermelo; this projectile example is standard in Bolza and Kneser
ideas.where_published: E735 (posthumous 1811/1862); not in Euler's lifetime publications as far as I know

ideas.what: Comparison of the extremal arc with a broken path along verticals and the zero-cost axis
ideas.modern_name: Goldschmidt-type discontinuous (non-smooth) minimizer; degenerate Lagrangian at x=0

missed.claim: Euler explicitly ties the multiplicity and non-existence of extremals (gg<fh, gg>fh) to the reachability of a point by projectiles of fixed energy. The boundary case gg=fh is the longest throw, i.e. the envelope. He sees that the extremal on the envelope is beaten by another path. This is in effect a pre-Jacobi observation that minimality fails at the conjugate point (the envelope), though he explains it only by discontinuity.
missed.quote: Quoties ergo fuerit gg<fh, ob signum radicale semper duo exhiberi poterunt minima, sive ab F ad H binos arcus parabolicos ducere licebit
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical priority for the envelope/conjugate-point phenomenon in the calculus of variations, and for Goldschmidt-type discontinuous solutions. Its importance depends on whether histories (e.g. Goldstine, Fraser) already discuss E735, which I am unsure of.

deep.surprise_reason: The algebra on this page is routine and correct. The interest lies in the surrounding argument: an Euler-era recognition of two extremals, the envelope, and a broken path beating the extremal. This anticipates Jacobi and Goldschmidt but is probably noted by at least some historians of the calculus of variations.
